Lena to run quantization / latency playbook and send benchmark notes by 2025-05-07
Marco to schedule internal follow-up enablement with AE team on 2025-05-06
action_items: Samir: produce 30s elevator pitch variants and attach in GDrive (due 2025-05-02)

summary: Internal enablement: AE+SE practice on discovery probing and demo choreography for BrightPath. Focus areas: precision messaging for cost/latency tradeoffs, clarifying Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private options, quick technical rebuttals (KV cache, quantization, rollout), and objection handling for procurement/security. Ended with concrete next steps and action items.
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: okay rolling, uh this is the probe and prove workshop, we're gonna run through the 30 second pitch, do a demo cold start, and then do rapid role play with some objections. any quick notes before we start?
[00:18] Lena: just that we should call out the specific win theme — production economics — like cost per token and predictable tail-latency. avoid too much model-lore.
[00:35] Marco: I'll time the pitch and keep notes on micro-benchmarks we want the SE to call out.
[00:45] Samir: cool. Jordan from BrightPath is playing the buyer in two scenarios. Jordan's brief: platform lead, cares about latency SLOs and audit logs. Renee will be the ML engineer asking quantization questions. Tom, solutions arch, will be procurement/security persona.
[01:10] (laughter) Jordan: yep i'm ready, play me.
[01:25] Samir (pitch, timed): "Redwood gives your engineering teams a single runtime that makes inference predictable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — you get consistent latency, cost controls like batching and cache, and auditing so you can meet SOC2 and internal security requirements without building ops yourself."
[01:45] Lena: couple things — drop 'inference' once, swap to "production-ready inference" and mention "rollouts" and "automatic fallback" very quickly. you spoke too many words about 'cost' — make it more tangible e.g., "reduce per-token spend by up to 30% via cache and batching".
[02:10] Samir: good. retake?
[02:18] Samir (v2): "Redwood is production-ready inference for teams: same API across hosted, dedicated, or private, predictable tail-latency, built-in rollouts and fallbacks, and cost controls like batching and KV cache that reduce token spend."
[02:36] Marco: 28 seconds, good. now demo cold start — Lena you lead.
[02:48] Lena: i'll start the console, quick note: we'll demo a chat call, show streaming tokens, then flip to routing policies and a quick metrics trace.
[03:05] [sound of window clicks] Lena: ok invoking a chat generate call, set model to rwin-1.2 (note: transcription may say rwin), streaming on. watch the token stream and the latency panel on the right.
[03:28] Jordan (buyer): how do you quantize that model without breaking quality?
[03:36] Lena: great question — we use model-level quantization profiles with A/B rollout. you can pin a control group to full precision and route 10% traffic to a quantized profile; monitor our eval hooks tied to your prompt set. if you see regressions it auto-rolls back.
[04:05] Renee (engineer): when you say 'cache' is that KV cash? excuse me, KV cash, like what's cached exactly? the prompt, embeddings, or what?
[04:18] Lena: yes sorry transcription. KV cache — we cache key/value attention states for long-running conversations and also prefix caching for common prompts. prefix cache reduces repeat token generation for known scaffolding.
[04:40] Samir: and this is where we show the numbers — sample: prefix cache reduced token egress by 24% for a customer with repeated prompts. mention that caching works across hosted and dedicated, but private on-prem requires configuration to persist cache based on customer policy.
[05:05] [05:05] Tom (procurement): security — we need SAML SSO, KMS integration, and an audit trail for model invocations. can you show where that lives?
[05:20] Lena: yes SSO via SAML or OIDC, RBAC at the token/route level, and audit logs are available both via console and a streaming export to your SIEM. KMS/HSM integrations for key management on Private deployments — we have a packaging step for air-gapped installs.
[05:50] Jordan: where does Redwood differ from Anthropic or OpenAI when it comes to enterprise installs?
[06:05] Samir: quick framing: many providers focus on model access; we focus on serving. Redwood gives you the runtime primitives — batching, KV cache, quantization profiles, routing policies, and an ops layer for rollouts and traceability. that means you trade less engineer time, get predictable tail latency, and have built-in rollback for quality regressions.
[06:35] Lena: also call out the Dedicated offering — reserved GPU pools that give throughput SLAs vs hosted which is best for time-to-value. Private is for data residency and regulated workloads.
[06:55] Jordan: ok role play 1: i'm skeptical of dedicated cost. push me.
[07:05] Samir (role): "I get the cost concern — can you share your p50/p95 token volumes?"
[07:12] Jordan: i don't have precise numbers right now, high-level: bursty traffic with steady background inference for our analytics pipelines.
[07:20] Lena: in that case we suggest hybrid routing: use Hosted for spiky, Dedicated for baseline, automatic fallback to a smaller quantized variant during peaks to maintain latency SLO. show them the routing slide.
[07:40] [click] Samir: and the math example: reserved capacity at 60% of steady load plus hosted burst reduces total cost vs overprovisioning dedicated. highlight Optimize recommendations — batching and per-model quantization will lower unit cost.
[08:05] Renee: can you walk me through how model rollouts integrate with deploy pipelines and CI?
[08:15] Lena: yep, we have a CLI and API for model pushes. you create a version, attach evals/prompt set, and define a rollout policy—canary, linear, or A/B. metrics are captured (latency, regressions, hallucination rate) and you can auto-failover to previous version.
[08:40] Jordan: quick objection — our security team cares about log retention and PII redaction, how configurable is that?
[08:50] Marco: we keep retention policies configurable per account, with the option to disable logging for specific routes. PII redaction hooks are available and we can integrate custom filters at the customer side in Private deployments.
[09:15] Samir: okay pivot — rapid-fire rebuttals. Lena will read a prompt and Jordan will throw a buyer objection.
[09:25] Lena: objection: "we already built inference in-house; why pay?"
[09:30] Samir: restate: "you own that IP, fine. but building and maintaining the serving layer, ops tooling, kernel tuning for GPUs, and safe rollouts is costly — Redwood buys you 9–12 months of engineering time and gives you predictable economics while keeping model freedom."
[09:55] Jordan: hmm show me the numbers, metrics or case study.
[10:00] Marco: quick reference: a retail customer reduced token cost by 28% and dropped mean latency 35% after moving to a dedicated footprint plus caching. we have the PDF; Samir will attach.
[10:20] [10:20] Lena: demo pivot — show the console trace for a 512 token conversation. latency p95, token billing, CPU/GPU utilization.
[10:35] [keyboard clack] Lena: here you can see continuous batching queues and where we cut in a KV cache hit. note the sudden dip in token egress after prefix match.
[11:05] Renee: about continuous batching — does it add latency for single-user interactive calls?
[11:12] Lena: batching has knobs: latency-first vs throughput-first. interactive paths use latency-first policy with small batch windows to avoid added latency. throughput heavy pipelines can use larger windows.
[11:35] Jordan: what about model compatibility — will older transformer variants work with your runtime?
[11:42] Lena: we onboard model families — transformer variants are fine, we do kernel selection and sometimes small model surgery for quantization friendliness. if a model is exotic we do an initial compatibility pass.
[12:05] Samir: ok moving on to messaging finesse — exercise: 1 minute to answer "why Redwood?" in a way that sales reps can memorize.
[12:18] Samir (practice): "Redwood is the serving platform for teams who care about predictable inference economics and reliability — same API across hosted, dedicated, and private, built-in caching, batching, rollouts, and auditability so you ship faster and keep latency and costs predictable."
[12:40] Lena: tighten — cut filler 'who care about' to 'that need', and change 'ship faster' to 'lower ops burden'.
[12:55] Samir (v2): "Redwood is the serving platform for teams that need predictable inference economics and reliability — one API across hosted, dedicated, and private, with caching, batching, rollouts, and auditability to lower ops burden and guarantee latency SLOs."
[13:15] Marco: good. now objection practice: Tom will read a procurement line about contracts and SLAs.
[13:25] Tom: "we need a 99.95% SLA, and penalties — can you commit?"
[13:30] Samir: we offer SLA-backed Dedicated contracts with uptime and latency targets; exact terms are negotiable and depend on committed capacity. for hosted we provide best-effort SLAs and enterprise packages for private installs include stricter legal terms.
[13:55] Tom: how do you prove latency historically?
[14:00] Lena: we provide token-level traces, historical p50/p95 dashboards per model, and can run a short benchmark during pilot. we also offer tracing hooks to instrument in your telemetry.
[14:25] [14:25] Jordan: quick pivot to competitor knock — what if buyer says Anthropic has better safety guardrails?
[14:35] Samir: acknowledge: Anthropic focuses on model safety and alignment. reply: Redwood complements safety-first models by providing serving controls and rollback hooks so you can run safe models reliably at scale. we emphasize that our focus is serving and ops, not building base models.
[15:00] Lena: next part is a mock live demo where the SE intentionally introduces a latency spike and we roleplay the escalation.
[15:12] [sound cue] Lena: triggering an artificial load now, you should see p95 jump.
[15:30] Jordan: yep p95 up. as buyer i'm freaking out.
[15:35] Samir: calm: "we have auto-fallback — we can route to a smaller quantized variant or another region, and we can throttle non-essential routes. we'll open an incident and provide a post-mortem with latency traces."
[15:55] Tom: what about billing spikes during incident?
[16:02] Marco: billing is usage-based; for Dedicated we model commit bands to avoid surprise spikes, and we can put guardrails to prevent runaway billing.
[16:25] [16:25] Lena: time check — about 60 minutes left in workshop, let's do lightning rebuttals.
[16:34] Lena (reads): "Objection: we need on-prem only."
[16:40] Samir: we provide Private deployment with a customer-managed control plane and optional air-gapped packaging. integrations like KMS/HSM and on-prem audit export are supported. the lift depends on your environment and we staff a deployment engineering engagement.
[17:00] Renee: technical deep dive: what GPU types do you support and how do you pick kernels?
[17:06] Lena: we support common GPU families (A100, H100, and some Graviton-like inference shapes on cloud) and kernel selection is automated based on model arch, sequence length, and quantization profile. we also provide a compatibility report per model.
[17:35] Samir: okay now split practice — Samir on discovery questions, Lena on technical clarifications. we'll simulate 3 buyer personas: Platform, ML Eng, Procurement.
[17:50] [roleplay snippets omitted for brevity but practiced — transcription continues]
[30:00] Samir: mid-workshop recap — we practiced pitch, demo, rebuttals, and showed a short trace and rollback. next we will finalize battle cards and the 30s elevator variants.
[30:20] Marco: reminder to attach the bench spreadsheet and the customer case PDF.
[30:30] (background typing)
[31:05] Lena: small note — use the phrase 'predictable tail-latency' not 'consistent tails' or you'll confuse buyer.
[31:30] Samir: good, will update deck.
[32:00] Jordan: last role play: i'm a skeptical ML engineer, push me on hallucination detection and evals.
[32:12] Samir: we attach prompt sets and regression alerts to every rollout; if hallucination spikes on your prompts the system flags it and can auto-roll back. we also support human-in-the-loop feedback sinks to feed into model evals.
[32:45] Renee: what's the easiest way to run an eval harness?
[32:50] Lena: we provide a small open-source harness and a hosted runner — you can run locally against your prompt set then upload results.
[33:15] Samir: okay final segment — choreography for a real customer call: who says what, slide handoffs, and post-call deliverables.
[33:30] Marco: AE opens, SE shows a live demo if invited, CSM closes and sets pilot. recommended cadence: discovery -> pilot (2 weeks) -> benching -> Dedicated sizing conversation.
[33:50] Samir: role calls: Samir opens; Lena takes technical deep-dive; Marco closes with next-step ask.
[34:10] [34:10] Jordan: as buyer i'd want a pilot with a 2-week bench and a short set of cust-specific prompts.
[34:20] Samir: agreed. we'll propose that in the follow-up.
[34:30] Lena: quick note about artifacts: attach 'pilot-workbook.xlsx' and 'security-onepager.pdf' and include a recorded demo clip with timestamps for the key moments.
[34:50] Marco: scheduling: Marco to send calendar invites for follow-ups.
[35:05] Samir: wrap — big takeaways: keep pitch short, call out production economics, demo the rollback/trace, and be ready with benchmarks and SOC2 artifacts.
[35:22] Jordan: thanks team, this was useful.
[35:30] (multiple people: thanks)
[35:40] Samir: end of recording — additional chatter not transcribed.
[75:00] [end of call]
